Hugh Miller
hyoo mil'ər
n. (Hugh Miller, 1802–1856, Cromarty stonemason, geologist, and editor of The Witness, the Free Church newspaper)
English occupational surname Miller, one who grinds grain; Hugh, from Germanic hug, mind, spirit.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Hugh Miller was a stonemason from Cromarty who taught himself geology from the quarries he worked and became the most widely read scientific writer in Scotland. The Old Red Sandstone and The Testimony of the Rocks were written in a prose that carried fossil fish and Devonian strata into ordinary households. At the Disruption he was made editor of The Witness, the Free Church's Edinburgh newspaper, and his leading articles did as much as any pulpit to carry the church's case to the Scottish public. He held that the geological record is of great antiquity and read the days of Genesis as long periods or as a sequence of prophetic visions, arguing the position against both the sceptics who used geology against Scripture and the developmentalists of the Vestiges school. He died by his own hand in December 1856, under an illness of the brain that his physicians certified. Job 38:4 is the question his whole subject stands under, “Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 38:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines geology as the science of the structure of the earth, and a fossil as a substance dug out of the earth.

expand to see more

GEOL'OGY, n. The doctrine or science of the structure of the earth or terraqueous globe, and of the substances which compose it.

FOS'SIL, n. A substance dug from the earth; in modern usage, the petrified remains of plants and animals.

STRA'TUM, n. A bed; a layer; a course; as a stratum of sand, of clay, or of earth.

Psa 104:24 — "O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all: the earth is full of thy riches."

Modern Corruption

The Free Church's best writer was a self-taught quarryman who read the rocks and would not read them against Scripture.

expand to see more

The dictionary's own position on Genesis is six literal days of twenty-four hours, and Miller did not hold it; he read the days as long ages and later as a series of visions shown to Moses. That reading is not the dictionary's voice. It is, however, the old-earth position within the Reformed line rather than a concession to unbelief, and Miller's entire purpose in holding it was apologetic: he was answering men who used the strata to argue that Scripture is a fable, and he never once granted that the record of the rocks may overrule the record of revelation.

What is worth recovering is the target of his heaviest fire. Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation had just proposed a universal development of life by natural law, and Miller attacked it from the fossil evidence itself, showing that the record exhibits sudden fully-formed appearances rather than the gradual ascent the theory required. Rom 1:20 is the ground he stood on, that the invisible things of God are “clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made” (Rom 1:20). His death was the end of a diagnosed illness and the dictionary records it plainly and without verdict, as the Free Church did when it buried him in the Grange with his elders carrying the coffin.

Usage

"“Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 38:4) — the question over the quarry."

"“in wisdom hast thou made them all” (Psa 104:24) — what he saw in the strata."

"“clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made” (Rom 1:20) — his apologetic ground."
